kf1.tip: Explain to a Year 7, in 30 words or fewer, why a bacterium is prokaryotic but an onion cell is eukaryotic. Use the words nucleus, loop of DNA and plasmid.
kf1.note: A good answer: a bacterium has no nucleus, so its DNA is a single loop floating in the cytoplasm, sometimes with small extra rings called plasmids. An onion cell is a plant cell, so its DNA is enclosed inside a nucleus. The key difference is whether the DNA sits inside a nucleus. If you only said bacteria are smaller, you missed the point the task asks for.

kf2.tip: Name the odd one out of animal cell, plant cell and bacterial cell for a cell wall, then again for mitochondria. Say why each time.
kf2.note: For a cell wall, the animal cell is the odd one out. Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall and bacteria also have a cell wall, but animal cells have none. For mitochondria, the bacterial cell is the odd one out, because animal and plant cells both have them and bacteria do not. The trap is picking the bacterial cell both times just because it is the prokaryote.

kf3.tip: Suppose plant cells lost their meristem tissue at the root and shoot tips. Say what would happen to a cutting from that plant, and why.
kf3.note: The cutting would not grow into a new plant. Meristems hold undifferentiated cells at the root and shoot tips, and these are what let plant cells keep differentiating throughout life. Without them, the cutting has no cells able to become the new specialised cells it needs. A strong answer names differentiation and links it to meristem tissue. A weaker answer just says the plant dies, without explaining why.

kf4.tip: Predict whether a light or an electron microscope could show ribosomes. Then check your answer against the 200 nm and 0.2 nm resolution figures.
kf4.note: Only an electron microscope could show ribosomes. The lesson names ribosomes as a structure electron microscopes let biologists see. A light microscope's resolution of about 200 nm is a thousand times coarser than the electron microscope's 0.2 nm, so it cannot pick out such tiny structures. If you chose the light microscope because ×1,500 sounds big, remember resolution, not magnification, decides how fine the detail is.

kf5.tip: Order the slide steps from placing onion epidermis to using the fine focus knob, then pick the step whose skipping would most spoil the image and say why.
kf5.note: The order is: place the specimen on the slide, add water or a stain, lower the coverslip at an angle, clip the slide on and select the lowest power objective, use the coarse focus, then the fine focus. Most pick the coverslip step, because trapped air bubbles distort the image. Skipping the stain is a fair case too, as structures become hard to see. The trap is naming a step without saying what goes wrong with the image.

cs1.tip: Rank nucleus, mitochondria, cell membrane and ribosomes by how badly a muscle cell would cope without each. Defend each place in one line.
cs1.note: Most would put mitochondria first, because a muscle cell needs lots of energy for contraction and mitochondria are where aerobic respiration transfers it. A strong answer also sees that the nucleus and ribosomes are linked: the nucleus holds the instructions for proteins and ribosomes make them, so losing either stops protein synthesis. The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves. The trap is listing each organelle's job without tying it to how a muscle cell works.
